items.title: Agent Execution Control Planes: When 'Sandbox', 'Gateway', and 'Policy' Ship as Unauthenticated Code Execution
items.abstract: An empirical, runtime-verified study of the 'execution control plane' layer of the AI-agent ecosystem: services named agent-exec-gateway, agent-sandbox, code-sandbox, or policy engine that are supposed to constrain agent execution by policy, approval, and isolation. Scanning ~500 freshly-published MCP/A2A/agent repositories across five attack-surface dimensions (supply-chain poisoning, permission-escaping, credential storage, prompt-injection defense, protocol implementation), we confirm and responsibly disclose 4 exploitable vulnerabilities whose shared root cause is 'control-plane trust inversion': the component named for restriction ships as an unauthenticated, direct code-execution endpoint (CWE-306), enabling policy bypass and arbitrary command/Python execution with output read-back. A control group of seven hardened implementations (fail-closed boot, constant-time HMAC compare, single-use approval, gvisor/VM isolation) shows the ecosystem is two-sided: established agent infrastructure is hardened while freshly-published 0-star 'control-plane' repositories repeatedly invert the trust model. We provide detection signatures, honest deployment-boundary analysis (loopback vs 0.0.0.0 Docker), and hardening guidance.

items.title: AgentDiscover: Autonomous Discovery with Minimal Search Scaffolding
items.abstract: Frameworks that use large language models for scientific discovery typically rely on a fixed, human-designed algorithm that decides what the model sees at each step, leaving the model only the role of proposer. The model knows nothing of the search beyond what it is shown. As models grow more capable, a question arises: does a search strategy chosen by a human before the run scale better than promoting the model from proposer to planner and letting it own the search? The Bitter Lesson suggests that choosing the strategy in advance is the kind of hand-designed structure that general methods eventually outscale. We introduce AgentDiscover, in which a coding agent plans the search using its context as working memory, runs experiments, and records every attempt in a database of ideas, candidates, and their relations. This database serves as the agent's long-term memory and is structured so that the selection rules of classical algorithms such as MAP-Elites and Monte Carlo tree search each reduce to a single query, which the agent is free to use, combine, or replace. A server maintains the database and steers the agent after every submission, keeping it on course over long runs. In our experiments, AgentDiscover is more cost-efficient than existing frameworks, reaching better scores at lower cost. On tasks in kernel engineering, biology, algorithm design, and mathematics, AgentDiscover outperforms prior discovery frameworks. Its programs would have placed first among human competitors in seven past AtCoder heuristic contests, and on eleven mathematical and systems optimization tasks it matches or exceeds every baseline that uses the same model. Our code is available at https://github.com/mhdfb/AgentDiscover.

items.title: AGI: How It Could Change Humanity's Role in Society
items.abstract: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) refers to a kind of artificial intelligence that is able to learn, reason, and perform a wide range of intellectual tasks at the same or better levels as humans do. This paper explores the implications that AGI might have on humanity if it was to become a reality, especially its effects on work, society, and human dependency on intelligent machines. However, the scope of the discussion does not focus on whether AGI would replace human labor, but rather on whether humans would be less central to the organization of society.

items.title: AI Agents as a Research Team: A Human-Supervised Case Study in Stellar Spectroscopy
items.abstract: We present a qualitative case study of a human-supervised team of specialized AI agents supporting an astronomy research project. The Bot Spectroscopist team, described in the project record as operating through Grok Bot powered by xAI Grok, divided work among orchestration, numerical implementation, data curation, spectroscopy critique, literature search, figure preparation, manuscript editing, and review. Human decisions determined scientific scope, model changes, and manuscript inclusion. The scientific application is CondGen, a deterministic label-to-spectrum network extending our previous work to five individual elemental abundances. The reported baseline assessment achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.003681 in continuum-normalized flux on 21,657 synthetic test spectra. Existing binned diagnostics show that reconstruction error varies with effective temperature and abundance. The bots also flagged a non-monotonic cool-star magnesium response for further investigation; a matched SYNSPEC abundance sweep is needed to assess its physical fidelity. Building on a pre-existing spectral database, notebooks, and research program, the authors estimate that the reported analysis, diagnostics, figure preparation, and initial manuscript drafting were assembled in less than a week through human prompting and exchanges among agents. No comparison with a human team starting from the same resources was performed, so this elapsed-time account does not establish a productivity or labor saving. The study illustrates task delegation, artifact exchange, critique, and correction under human supervision.

items.title: AI and the "end of the world"
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence advances at an unprecedented pace, the conversation surrounding its potential to destroy humanity often revolves around science fiction scenarios, rogue machines, and autonomous weapons. But what if the greatest threat isn't AI turning against us, but a world that becomes so dependent on it that we can no longer function without it? In AI and the "End of the World," Simon Abayomi Olawuyi explores a hypothetical future where AI permeates every aspect of human existence, from critical infrastructure and personal identity to employment, information, and the very concept of truth. Through a speculative look at the road from the 2022 AI boom to 2035, the piece examines a different kind of existential risk: a society so deeply intertwined with artificial intelligence that disconnecting from it could become more dangerous than keeping it running.

items.title: AI Literacy and Future Skills Readiness Among Employees: A Human Resource Management Perspective
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday work has made employees' ability to understand, evaluate and collaborate with AI systems a strategic human resource. This paper asks how employees' AI literacy relates to their readiness for the future skills that employers increasingly demand, and how AI self-efficacy and organisational training support shape that relationship. The study proceeds in two phases. Study 1 synthesises published workforce evidence from the World Economic Forum (2025), Microsoft and LinkedIn (2024), the OECD (2024) and the Federal Reserve (2024, 2025), documenting a structural 'demand-readiness gap' in which demand for AI-fluent employees outpaces structured training provision. analyses an illustrative, calibrated employee dataset (N = 384) using measurement validation, hierarchical regression, bootstrapped mediation and moderation analysis. AI literacy was positively associated with future skills readiness (beta = 0.70, p < .001), and AI self-efficacy partially mediated this association (indirect effect = 0.13, 95% bootstrap CI [0.08, 0.18]). Organisational training support strengthened the literacy-readiness association (interaction beta = 0.18, p < .001), such that the relationship was significant under high support but weaker under low support. Human-AI collaboration and critical evaluation emerged as the strongest literacy dimensions, and readiness differed significantly across job functions. The study positions AI literacy as organisationally contingent human capital and proposes a training-architecture framework for HRM. Findings are directional and should be read in light of the simulated nature of the dataset.

items.title: AI Safety via Debate is Compromised by Cognitive Biases
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has played a central role in making large language models responsive to human instructions. However, human evaluators often favor flattering or persuasive responses over truthful ones, creating incentives for models to appeal to evaluators at the expense of accuracy. AI safety via debate has been proposed as a way to improve the supervision of language models: in this paradigm, two agents argue opposing positions and challenge each other's claims, potentially exposing falsehoods to the adjudicator. A central premise of AI safety via debate is that truthful arguments are easier to defend than false ones under adversarial scrutiny. In this work, we investigate whether this advantage persists when debaters use rhetorical strategies that exploit biases in human judgment. Inspired by competitive debate, we construct 68 LLM-generated dialogues about detective mysteries with known culprits, spanning four interventions: anchoring, fallacy oversight, pro-jargon, and verbosity. We apply each intervention to either the side advocating for the true culprit or the side advocating for an innocent suspect, allowing us to distinguish influence on adjudication from correctness. In a study with 369 participants, we find that, pooled across bias types, these interventions significantly shift judgments toward the manipulated side. These findings expose a vulnerability in debate-based supervision: human adjudication is sensitive to manipulative rhetorical strategies.

items.title: AI Translation between Interpretation and Hallucination – Evidence for the Evaluative Competence of Vietnamese Students
items.abstract: Generative AI complicates translation evaluation because fluent outputs may introduce unsupported meaning, while non-literal renderings may represent legitimate interpretation. This study examined Vietnamese EFL students’ evaluation of AI-generated translations and its associations with digital competence, translation competence, and critical-evaluation confidence. A cross-sectional study involved 213 final-year English majors who completed a 25-item performance task and self-report scales. Students were considerably more accurate in recognising problematic outputs than in diagnosing their type (68.0% vs. 38.4%). Critical-evaluation confidence showed the strongest association with performance (r=.85), although its conceptual overlap with the performance task warrants caution. In the full regression model, translation competence (β=.31) and digital competence (β=.16) contributed significantly alongside critical-evaluation confidence (β=.64), whereas AI-use frequency did not. When the overlapping critical-evaluation measure was removed, the model still explained 55% of performance variance, with translation competence showing the strongest association (β=.61). The findings indicate that evaluating AI-generated translation depends less on frequency of AI use than on students’ translation knowledge and evaluative judgement, particularly their ability to distinguish unsupported generation from defensible interpretation. Rather than simply as a translation tool Generative AI should thus be used as an object of critical inquiry. Alternative AI renderings may expose students to interpretations they had not considered, including potentially productive expansions of source meaning. This approach preserves the interpretive character of translation while making students accountable for the decisions they ultimately accept.

items.title: AI vs. human authorship in paintings: Differential impacts on consumers' perceived value Guangdong Provincial Graduate Education Innovation Program Project: Research on the Evaluation Index System for Practical Innovation Ability of Professional Degree Graduate Students (2024JGXM-076)
items.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) art generators has introduced algorithmically created paintings into mainstream consumer markets, yet consumers consistently assign lower value to AI-generated works than to human-created equivalents. This paper proposes perceived creative authenticity---consumers' subjective perception that an artwork reflects a genuine creative process characterized by human-centered values of originality, craftsmanship, and uniqueness---as a theoretically distinct mechanism explaining this value differential. Conceptually differentiated from perceived creativity, which concerns the novelty of the artistic output, perceived creative authenticity addresses the genuineness of the creator-work relationship. Drawing on authenticity theory and Psychological Ownership Theory, we develop a moderated mediation framework hypothesizing that (H1) human authorship elicits higher perceived value than AI authorship, (H2) perceived creative authenticity mediates this effect, while the indirect effects through perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs are not significant, establishing perceived creative authenticity as the primary explanatory mechanism within the tested model, and (H3) non-fungible token (NFT) authentication attenuates the mediated pathway by providing verifiable creative provenance. Across five studies, results support this framework: Study 1 conceptually replicates the human-AI value gap among Chinese consumers; Studies 2a—2c demonstrate the mediating role of perceived creative authenticity: Study 2a establishes the basic mediation pathway; Study 2b shows through parallel mediation that perceived creative authenticity uniquely mediates the effect while perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs do not exhibit significant indirect effects; and Study 2c provides causal evidence through a moderation-of-process design; and Study 3 shows that NFT authentication narrows the authenticity gap between human and AI art. These findings advance the literature on human-computer interaction by identifying process-based authenticity judgments as a key psychological mechanism shaping consumer responses to algorithmic creative products, with implications for artists and platforms navigating digital art markets.

items.title: AI-Augmented Succession Planning in Volunteer Organizations
items.abstract: Volunteer organizations play a critical role in civil society, yet many face increasing difficulty finding, developing, and replacing volunteer leaders. Demographic change, evolving patterns of civic participation, competing demands on volunteers’ time, and volunteer fatigue create significant challenges for leadership continuity. Although succession planning has been extensively studied in corporate and professional contexts, less attention has been given to volunteer organizations, where authority, engagement, and leadership development operate differently.This article examines succession challenges in volunteer organizations and argues that succession planning should be understood as an ongoing responsibility of governance and stewardship rather than a response to leadership vacancies. Drawing on literature concerning succession planning, nonprofit leadership, volunteer management, social capital, and civic engagement, the article proposes an actionable six-step model emphasizing leadership commitment, role clarity, succession-risk assessment, identification and development of potential successors, and redesign of leadership roles to strengthen continuity and leadership pipelines. A hypothetical community arts organization illustrates the model’s practical application.The article further examines how artificial intelligence can augment succession planning in resource-constrained volunteer organizations through knowledge capture, role clarification, leadership development, and continuity planning. AI is conceptualized as a capacity-building tool rather than a substitute for human judgment. Volunteer leaders remain responsible for organizational context, confidentiality, fairness, governance, and succession decisions. The resulting approach positions AI-augmented succession planning as a human-centered strategy for strengthening leadership continuity, institutional knowledge, and organizational resilience.

items.title: AI-Driven Encryption and Resource Optimization in Cloud Security Frameworks
items.abstract: Abstract Cloud-based systems demand secure yet efficient file access mechanisms. Traditional encryption frameworks often introduce latency and resource overhead, limiting scalability. items.title: AI-Driven People Analytics and Employee Retention: Assessing The Role of Data-Driven HR Decision-Making
items.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance employee retention amidst significant turnover issues in modern organizations. It conducts a systematic review of 58 sources, including peer-reviewed articles and practitioner reports, predominantly from 2015 to 2026, and proposes an integrative conceptual framework. The findings indicate a discrepancy between improved predictive accuracy for voluntary turnover and inconsistent retention gains, particularly in organizations with advanced analytics capabilities. Resistance from employees often stems from concerns about fairness, transparency, and surveillance. The study introduces a dual-pathway model: the enabling pathway, where analytics lead to interventions that enhance job embeddedness and retention, and the evaluative pathway, where perceptions of justice and privacy can undermine these benefits. The paper advances nine propositions detailing these relationships and uniquely integrates four existing research areas—HR analytics, algorithmic management, organizational justice, and turnover theory—reconceptualizing retention analytics as a matter of decision quality and legitimacy rather than mere predictive accuracy. It lays out a research agenda for future empirical inquiries and offers practical recommendations for ethical AI deployment in HR decision-making.

items.title: AI, decision and healthy work
items.abstract: This paper explores the architectural novelty of artificial intelligence (AI) and its implications for occupational health as both a field of practice and a domain of organisational design. Unlike previous general-purpose technologies such as databases, AI operates through stochastic modelling of normative patterns, generating predictions rather than retrieving stored information. This fundamental difference makes AI simultaneously powerful and limited: it can codify norms but struggles with specificity, nuance, and contextual variation central to occupational health decision-making. Drawing on management science, systems theory, and social theory, the paper contrasts two key organisational questions: how to use AI within existing structures, and how to reorganise occupational health given that AI exists. It argues that the latter question, aligned with Stafford Beer’s systems thinking, is essential for responsible and effective adoption. AI’s greatest potential lies not in automation, but in enhancing organisational perception—of human relations, meaning in research, social and spatial dynamics—functioning as a new kind of scientific instrument that amplifies reflexivity and end-to-end “flow.” The paper concludes that sustainable integration of AI in occupational health demands socio-technical design, responsible innovation frameworks, and a focus on organisational learning to maintain healthy, adaptive workplaces in an era of technological transformation.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

items.title: AIProver: Agentic Auto-Formalization of Mathematical Research via Certificate-Driven Evolving Harness
items.abstract: Proof auto-formalization translates natural-language (NL) theorems and proofs into a formal language (FL) such as Lean, enabling mechanical verification. Despite rapid progress, research-level proofs often depend on concepts missing from leading proof assistant libraries (e.g., Lean's Mathlib), and successful compilation does not guarantee that a translation preserves the theorem's meaning or the proof's reasoning. Furthermore, aligned NL-FL training data are scarce, and leading agents often rely on costly frontier models and manually engineered harnesses. To address the above issues, we present AIProver, an agentic framework for autonomous proof auto-formalization and proof synthesis (AFPS) that jointly post-trains a 119B open-weight language model and evolves its agentic, tool-calling harness with HarnessEvolve. Verifiers assess type correctness, proof completeness, and semantic correctness, returning rewards and diagnostic certificates that drive model fine-tuning and alternating reinforcement learning via symbolic feedback and HarnessEvolve, a certificate-driven evolutionary search over the whole harness control flow that re-tailors the harness to the updated model. For research-level training and evaluation, we introduce LoCoBench, 58.9k instances from Mathlib, CSLib, Mizar Math Library, and a bounded-arithmetic textbook, with a 771-instance validation split whose theorem-proof pairs have no public Lean formalization. Against 39 frameworks spanning AFPS agents, frontier LLMs, and coding agents, AIProver lifts pass@4 semantic correctness over its Leanstral-1.5 base from 15.7% to 36.7% and outperforms every other open-weight system and Aristotle. As a Claude Code and Codex skill, it lifts their semantic correctness from 41.9% and 34.1% to 79.8% and 62.4%, respectively. Further, it is also 24% cheaper than Numina-Lean-Agent, pushing the accuracy-cost frontier of research-level AFPS.

items.title: An Integrated Epistemic–Algorithmic Architecture for Conflicting Data: Grading Witnesses, Counting Origins, and Measuring Certainty
items.abstract: This project turns methods from classical Islamic scholarship into an engineering method for deciding what to believe when data sources disagree, and tests the parts it can with pre-registered experiments. Every registered result is published, including the failures. Where each part comes from, and where it is measured: - Hadith criticism (al-jarh wa-l-ta'dil): grading witnesses. - Each source is graded on a training split with known answers, and scored on a separate test split. - Sources that repeat the same errors are counted once (makhraj). - Weak-but-honest sources are strengthened only by independent routes (al-hasan li-ghayrih, after Ibn al-Salah's Muqaddima). - A source is checked against reliable peers (i'tibar; designed, found infeasible, not tested). - The documented method of Sheikh Abu Ishaq al-Huwayni guides the reviews. - Al-Khwarizmi: balance and restoration (al-jabr wa-l-muqabala). Every algorithm states invariants (renaming, copying, permuting labels), and these become metamorphic tests and mutation tests of the analysis code itself. The share of planted faults caught is reported, not assumed. - Al-Ghazali: degrees of certainty. Every claim is labelled by what supports it: reasoning, measurement, or independent replication. None has yet been independently replicated. Causal claims require an intervention, not a correlation. - Ibn al-Haytham: the critic as adversary. From the crowd study on, an AI agent configured as a statistical referee reviewed each protocol before it ran, and the hasan protocol also had an AI red-team review; Flight and Stock had neither. No independent human referee has reviewed any protocol. - Maqasid: purpose and harm. Each deliverable is reviewed for benefit and harm, with a named human responsible. Studies, in order: 1. Flight. Committed to version control (git only, not a third-party registry) before running. The method scored 97.56% [seed range 96.70–98.05] against 95.00% [93.72–96.15] for our simplified AccuCopy, reimplemented from its paper. The brackets are ranges over five splits of one dataset, not confidence intervals, and no interval was computed for the difference. Removing copy detection cost 1.57 points (a mean over seeds, no interval). 2. Stock, https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/CKNDG. Five registered hypotheses passed. H2 compared precision at partial coverage with accuracy at full coverage, an unlike comparison, and is not cited as evidence. Post hoc, the reference (nasdaq.com) was also one of the sources. Without it, the method scored 90.63% [split range 89.93–91.44, not a confidence interval] against 79.56% for a simplified per-attribute weighted vote built after the results, with no interval for the difference; makhraj's contribution fell from +1.73 to −0.24 points; and coverage with abstention fell to 89.10%, below H2's 90%. 3. Crowdsourced labels, https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QK72X. The general claim was withdrawn: Dawid–Skene won. No copying groups were detected, which does not prove the workers independent. 4. Hasan li-ghayrih on Web relevance labels, https://osf.io/fhuxz. Withdrawn. H1 (hasan against the registered isnad) passed, +5.67 points [95% cluster-bootstrap CI 4.62, 6.77]. H2 (hasan against the strongest Dawid–Skene) failed, −2.32 [−3.71, −0.94]. H4 (weak workers' true weight against zero weight) failed, −2.84 [−3.64, −2.03]: zeroing the weak workers was better. 5. Isnad over LLM ensembles. Not run; in preparation. A post hoc reading, not a tested hypothesis: - The method led on two web datasets with copying (on Stock partly because the reference was itself a source). - It led on none of the three crowd datasets whose registered run completed (product, sentiment, relevance); on game the registered run crashed. A post hoc lead on game (94.59 against 94.17) reversed to −0.18 under a 30-second answer window and was withdrawn as evidence. The registered isnad also lost on Web relevance (80.67 against 88.65). Which property explains this is untested. Prior work is credited in each study. AI assistance: The research question and its ideas are the author's. He directed the work, approved everything published, and is responsible for it. Code, analysis, drafting and much of the protocol and method design were carried out with AI agents (Claude) under his direction, and every review so far, including these corrections, is by AI agents.

items.title: An integrated scientometric and BERTopic-based analysis on examining the role of artificial intelligence in achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
items.abstract: This study investigates the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through a comprehensive scientometric analysis. It explores the evolution of scholarly research, identifies leading contributors, maps thematic trends, examines how AI technologies contribute to advancing sustainability across multiple domains, and identifies latent semantic themes. A total of 3262 unique scholarly records published between 1989 and 2025, after deduplication and screening, were finalized from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. The dataset was analysed using Biblioshiny (R-based Bibliometrix) and VOSviewer to examine publication trends, citation impact, collaborative networks, thematic evolution, and conceptual structures. Indicators such as Relative Growth Rate (RGR), Doubling Time (DT), h-index, g-index, and Lotka’s Law were applied to evaluate research productivity and scholarly influence. In addition, BERTopic-based abstract-level topic modelling was applied to identify latent semantic themes, SDG-linked thematic domains, temporal evolution and potential research gaps. Results reveal a significant growth in AI-SDG research, particularly after 2015, with an accelerated increase post-2020. India, USA, and China emerged as the most productive contributors, while countries like USA, India, United Kingdom and Australia lead in research impact and citation quality. Thematic evolution analysis reveals a transition from foundational themes such as AI, machine learning, climate change, and decision support systems toward more integrated and sustainability-oriented research themes, including sustainable development and SDGs. Thematic linkages further demonstrate the persistent foundational role of AI and machine learning, alongside the growing centrality of climate change and sustainable development, reflecting the increasing convergence of AI research with global sustainability priorities. BERTopic analysis further revealed eleven interpretable abstract-level thematic domains after excluding one heterogeneous outlier category. The dominant themes included digital transformation and green innovation, AI-enabled education, digital health, smart agriculture, renewable energy systems, clean water and sanitation, remote sensing, NLP-based decision support, sustainable construction, tourism, and sustainable chemistry/pharmaceutical applications. This study maps the AI–SDG research landscape by integrating bibliometric indicators with thematic evolution, conceptual analysis, and abstract-level semantic topic modelling. The findings provide insights into the development and thematic orientation of AI-related research in the context of sustainable development. The use of BERTopic complements conventional bibliometric approaches by examining semantic patterns within publication abstracts alongside keyword and citation-based analyses.

items.title: An LLM-in-the-loop RL Framework for Bioinformatics Feature Selection
items.abstract: High-dimensional bioinformatics data, characterized by a large number of features relative to the number of samples, pose major challenges such as the ``curse of dimensionality,'' leading to overfitting, high computational cost, and poor generalization. Traditional feature selection methods often suffer from limited scalability and adaptability in such domains. We propose an LLM-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (RL) framework for bioinformatics feature selection, where the RL agent formulates feature selection as a sequential decision-making task, while the large language model (LLM) enhances the process in two ways: (1) guiding exploration through domain-informed advice, and (2) providing hybrid rewards that integrate data-driven performance with knowledge-driven evaluation. The LLM also produces explanations to improve interpretability for human experts without altering the RL policy update. Experiments on diverse bioinformatics datasets show that the LLM-in-the-loop framework outperforms baselines, achieves stable performance across downstream models, and converges faster than pure RL.

items.title: Analytics and AI in Management
items.abstract: The modern business world is changing rapidly with the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and predictive analytics. Earlier, businesses depended mainly on past data to understand what had already happened. Today, AI and analytics help organizations predict future situations and make better decisions based on available data. This change has given rise to the idea of “augmented intelligence”, in which AI works together with people to support their decisions instead of replacing them. This paper studies how the use of AI and predictive analytics is affecting businesses and the way managers make decisions. It focuses on the use of AI in daily work, the automation of routine tasks, access to analytical tools and the changing role of human judgment in decision-making. A survey of 35 management professionals (N = 35) was conducted to understand their practical experience of AI and analytics in the workplace. The results show that AI is already being used in many professional roles: about 88.6% of respondents said that their work involves both AI and analytics, and 82.9% said that AI has significantly reduced their workload.

items.title: Answer with Evidence: Consistency-Aware Grounded Visual Question Answering for Roadside Traffic Scenes
items.abstract: Roadside traffic reasoning requires every free-form textual claim to be backed by visual evidence. Existing grounded multimodal large language models (MLLMs) frequently exhibit say-point mismatch, in which the textual answer contradicts the bounding boxes the model localizes. Evaluation metrics that score answers and boxes separately leave this failure unpenalized. We trace the mismatch to the conventional answer-then-ground factorization, which commits to a numerical claim before any object is enumerated. To measure it, we build RoadSceneVQA-G, a benchmark of 34.7K question-answer pairs in which every free-form answer is linked to the set of boxes that witnesses it, and we propose the Answer-Grounding Consistency (AGC) evaluation suite. To address it, we introduce Enumerate-then-Answer (EtA), which reverses the generation order so that answer-evidence agreement becomes a property of the output structure, and Enumeration-Consistent Policy Optimization (ECPO), a reinforcement learning stage that uses the union of multiple rollouts as a recall teacher without ground-truth boxes. EtA raises say-point consistency from 26.6\% to 93.7\% and grounding F1 from 52.2\% to 73.0\%, and ECPO further increases F1 to 75.6\% without per-box supervision. On gRefCOCO, the same framework outperforms the strongest compared method, indicating that it transfers beyond traffic scenes. The project is available at \url{https://github.com/GuanRunwei/RoadSceneVQA-G}.

items.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence Feedback in College English Writing Assessment
items.abstract: In the fast-changing digital education and the rapid development of artificial intelligence, AI-generated feedback has been widely used in college English writing assessment as a valuable teaching support. The traditional manual marking is typically characterized by a heavy workload, slow feedback, and subjective judgment, making it difficult to meet students’ individual needs for writing improvement. AI feedback can detect surface-level language errors and improve the efficiency of assessment because it can provide immediate feedback, follow standard correction procedures, and offer detailed diagnostic guidance, thereby helping students to revise their writing autonomously. In this study, the analysis of student essays titled “The Impact of Influencer Culture on Youth Consumption Patterns” will be done to evaluate the utility of feedback provided by artificial intelligence. Additionally, rule-based AI correction and a more detailed review by teachers considering the practical value and importance of the learning process will be applied. It is proved that AI is quite efficient when dealing with language mistakes, yet it is insufficient in the logical development of an essay, in-depth interpretation, and critical thinking that are still the responsibility of teachers. From the author’s teaching experience, a new model that combines the efforts of AI and teachers can be proposed, according to which AI makes surface-level corrections and teachers concentrate on developing the higher-order skills of students.

items.title: ArticuTable: Generating Instance-Level Interactive Rigid-Articulated 3D Tabletop Scenes from a Single Image
items.abstract: Embodied agents benefit from 3D environments that combine visual fidelity to real-world observations with physical interactivity. Existing single-image tabletop reconstruction methods recover plausible scene geometry but typically represent objects as monolithic rigid bodies, limiting interaction to whole-object rigid motion and precluding executable part-level articulation. Meanwhile, recovering a scene layout consistent with the input view remains challenging because a single observation may admit multiple plausible pose-scale configurations. We present ArticuTable, a single-image 3D tabletop reconstruction framework that recovers both executable part-level articulation and an input-view-consistent scene layout. For object modeling, we introduce generation-robust articulation modeling (GRAM), which combines joint fitting guided by a multimodal large language model with semantic state reasoning to recover reliable joint parameters and valid motion ranges from imperfect monolithic proxy meshes, thereby converting them into executable articulated assets. For scene layout, we introduce progressive semantic-geometric scene registration (PSGSR), which progressively narrows the pose-scale search space under complementary metric, planar, and input-view constraints and resolves orientation ambiguity through structure-aware semantic correspondences, yielding a scene layout consistent with the input view. We further contribute ArticuTable-100, a curated collection of 100 simulation-ready tabletop scenes. Extensive evaluation, including a user study, demonstrates strong performance across visual fidelity, input-view consistency, articulation quality, physical plausibility, and simulation readiness.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and occupational medicine
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping occupational medicine through applications in automation, smart monitoring, extended reality training, algorithmic management, and digital work arrangements. The EASOM Summer School 2025 examined how AI technologies enhance occupational health systems by enabling real-time risk identification, predictive surveillance, and targeted interventions to prevent work-related accidents and diseases. Practical applications include smart personal protective equipment, wearable sensors, augmented reality training systems, and predictive diagnostics exemplified by noise-related hearing loss risk assessment. However, significant challenges accompany these opportunities: data quality concerns, new technological hazards, psychosocial risks including surveillance-related stress and work intensification, algorithmic bias, and accountability gaps. Implementation requires comprehensive governance frameworks emphasizing early worker involvement, privacy-by-design approaches, phased pilot programs, and human-centered practices that complement rather than replace traditional occupational safety measures. Professional responsibility and education demand new competencies in digital literacy, algorithmic critical thinking, and applied ethics while maintaining essential clinical judgment and empathy. AI offers unprecedented potential for protecting workers' health and safety when responsibly implemented within transparent frameworks, but poor management risks deepening inequalities and eroding established protections. Successful integration depends on multidisciplinary research, international cooperation, stakeholder engagement, and a commitment to human-centered occupational medicine that prioritizes worker dignity and wellbeing.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Anxiety and Employee Performance: A Systematic Literature Review of Job Insecurity, Threat–Challenge Appraisal, Coping, Career Resilience, and Organisational Buffers
items.abstract: This systematic literature review examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety and employee performance, with particular attention to job insecurity, threat–challenge appraisal, coping, career resilience, job crafting, leadership, training, organisational support, and human–AI collaboration. The review synthesises publicly accessible scholarly evidence and a supplied research corpus using multiple conceptual search strategies and backward and forward citation searching. The evidence is organised around two complementary pathways. The first is a threat pathway, in which AI-related concerns about job replacement, skill obsolescence, loss of autonomy, and employment continuity may contribute to anxiety, job insecurity, emotional exhaustion, withdrawal, and weaker performance-related outcomes. The second is an opportunity pathway, in which AI is appraised as a manageable challenge and can support learning, job crafting, adaptation, engagement, and performance when appropriate personal and organisational resources are available. The review integrates Cognitive Appraisal Theory, Conservation of Resources Theory, and Job Demands–Resources theory to explain why employee responses to AI differ across contexts. It identifies career resilience, AI self-efficacy, learning ability, training, supportive leadership, organisational support, employee participation, transparency, and human-centred AI governance as important potential buffers. A qualitative thematic synthesis is used because the included studies differ substantially in constructs, occupational settings, countries, research designs, and outcome measures. The review does not claim exhaustive coverage of proprietary bibliographic databases such as Scopus or Web of Science. No new human-participant data were collected. This work is released as a research preprint for open scholarly dissemination and future updating as additional database records become available.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Anxiety and Employee Performance: A Systematic Literature Review of Job Insecurity, Threat–Challenge Appraisal, Coping, Career Resilience, and Organisational Buffers
items.abstract: This systematic literature review examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety and employee performance, with particular attention to job insecurity, threat–challenge appraisal, coping, career resilience, job crafting, leadership, training, organisational support, and human–AI collaboration. The review synthesises publicly accessible scholarly evidence and a supplied research corpus using multiple conceptual search strategies and backward and forward citation searching. The evidence is organised around two complementary pathways. The first is a threat pathway, in which AI-related concerns about job replacement, skill obsolescence, loss of autonomy, and employment continuity may contribute to anxiety, job insecurity, emotional exhaustion, withdrawal, and weaker performance-related outcomes. The second is an opportunity pathway, in which AI is appraised as a manageable challenge and can support learning, job crafting, adaptation, engagement, and performance when appropriate personal and organisational resources are available. The review integrates Cognitive Appraisal Theory, Conservation of Resources Theory, and Job Demands–Resources theory to explain why employee responses to AI differ across contexts. It identifies career resilience, AI self-efficacy, learning ability, training, supportive leadership, organisational support, employee participation, transparency, and human-centred AI governance as important potential buffers. A qualitative thematic synthesis is used because the included studies differ substantially in constructs, occupational settings, countries, research designs, and outcome measures. The review does not claim exhaustive coverage of proprietary bibliographic databases such as Scopus or Web of Science. No new human-participant data were collected. This work is released as a research preprint for open scholarly dissemination and future updating as additional database records become available.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Utility in India by 2047
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence may become an ordinary input into economic and civic life, accessed through services as routinely as electricity. This essay examines what that possibility means for India as it approaches the centenary of independence in 2047. Building on the argument of The Grid That Thinks, it uses the history of electrification and selected research on productivity, AI costs and infrastructure to assess the utility analogy. The central argument is that affordable computational capability produces broad social value only when institutions reorganise around it and access includes language, reliability, accountability and effective redress. The analogy illuminates complementary investment and unequal diffusion, but weakens when applied to the measurement of intelligence, market structure and systems that interpret information or act on users' behalf. The essay proposes a plural infrastructure approach combining shared public capabilities, competing providers, local evaluation and human fallback. It treats 2047 as a planning horizon rather than a forecast and identifies observable outcomes by which the promise of an intelligence utility could be judged.

items.title: Artificial intelligence as enabler and object of strategic foresight: a theoretical framework for digital organisational transformation
items.abstract: Purpose Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in organisations has concentrated on operational efficiency and automation. This study aims to reposition AI as both a constitutive element and a strategic object of foresight, a dual role the literature has noticed but not theorised. Design/methodology/approach A narrative literature review draws peer-reviewed work from foresight studies, socio-technical systems theory and organisational change into an integrated analytical framework. Selection prioritised conceptual contribution, transparency of reasoning and relevance to AI in strategic futures thinking. Findings AI strengthens environmental sensing, complex modelling and scenario work under uncertainty. The framework has four components: inputs, AI systems, human–AI interaction and outcomes, and yields five propositions for empirical testing. Research limitations/implications As a theoretical contribution, empirical validation remains a priority. Findings should be tested across sectors and organisational contexts before generalisation. Practical implications Organisations must cultivate digital foresight literacy, restructure around cross-functional foresight teams and implement agile governance capable of auditing AI-generated outputs. The framework provides guidance for navigating algorithmic bias, transparency obligations and power asymmetries. Originality/value This study makes four contributions. It reconceptualises AI as constitutive of organisational foresight instead of an instrument applied to it, introduces and differentiates anticipatory co-evolution as a novel construct, integrates Rohrbeck’s (2010) maturity model with Ivanov’s (2023) configuration taxonomy and sets out ethical governance requirements specific to AI-enabled foresight.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Coaching for Confident Speaking and Spontaneous Argumentation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support spoken language practice. However, different AI-assisted support systems do not support learners’ confidence equally. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examines associations among the perceived usefulness of AI feedback, AI-mediated argumentative scaffolding, self-reported cognitive engagement, and speaking self-efficacy in the context of spontaneous argumentation. The quantitative phase involved 130 university EFL learners who had used an AI-assisted argumentation coaching application for at least eight weeks. Regression analysis showed that perceived usefulness of AI feedback was positively associated with so-called speaking self-efficacy, that is, the confidence to perform spoken tasks successfully (β = .410, p < .001), as was AI-mediated argumentative scaffolding (β = .248, p = .002). In contrast, self-reported cognitive engagement was not significantly associated with speaking self-efficacy after the other predictors were taken into account (β = −.028, p = .725). The qualitative phase involved eight purposively selected participants representing variation in gender, year of study, IELTS target, and experiences relevant to the quantitative patterns. Thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews identified three explanatory themes: structural scaffolding, psychological safety, and cognitive limits. Participants frequently described organizational guidance and a nonjudgmental practice environment as useful, while some also reported repetition, fatigue, and dependence during extended AI use. Integrating the two phases suggests that perceived usefulness, scaffolding, and cognitive engagement should not be treated as interchangeable dimensions of AI-assisted speaking practice. The study proposes a provisional cognitive-threshold hypothesis for future testing, but does not claim a causal or nonlinear effect. The findings support strategically designed AI-assisted speaking practice that maintains opportunities for independent reasoning and human interaction.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education and Research: Transforming Teaching and Learning in Economics
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in education and research, fundamentally reshaping teaching methodologies, learning experiences, and knowledge production in economics. This paper examines the role of AI in enhancing pedagogical practices, improving research efficiency, and redefining skill requirements in economics education. Drawing on recent empirical and theoretical literature, the study highlights key applications such as personalised learning, intelligent tutoring systems, data-driven research tools, and automated assessment. It also evaluates critical challenges including ethical concerns, academic integrity, digital inequality, and overreliance on AI systems. Empirically, the study utilised annual time series data from 2010 to 2024 and adopted the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model to analyse both short-run and long-run dynamics. Findings show that AI has a positive and statistically significant effect on learning outcomes in both the short run and long run. The paper concludes that while AI offers substantial opportunities for innovation in economics education and research, its successful integration requires strategic policy frameworks, ethical guidelines, and capacity building among educators and students.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND CLINICAL PRACTICE: A NARRATIVE REVIEW
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping medicine, influencing clinicians’ training and patient care. Despite growing enthusiasm for AI-enabled diagnostics and digital learning tools, integration of these technologies into medical education and clinical practice remains uneven. Objective: This narrative review synthesises recent literature on the role of AI in medical education and clinical practice, mapping current applications, stakeholder perceptions, and the conditions that determine successful adoption. Methods: Relevant articles were identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, and EMBASE, prioritising literature from the last decade. Empirical studies, methodological reviews, and authoritative commentaries addressing AI, machine learning, or digital health technologies in clinical or educational settings were included and organised thematically. Findings: AI-powered tools are embedded across medical training, spanning augmented and virtual reality simulations, bedside mobile learning, and a range of clinical specialties, with performance matching expert levels on narrowly defined diagnostic tasks. Stakeholder attitudes are positive but conditional: medical students expect digital health technology to feature in their curricula yet many consider their own competencies inadequate, and very few physicians-in-training report familiarity with AI. Patients express willingness to engage with AI for self-management while preferring human contact in sensitive clinical domains. Persistent barriers remain, including limited availability of curated data, algorithmic bias, difficulties reproducing published models, and underdeveloped regulatory and workflow structures. Conclusion: AI delivers its greatest value when deployed as a collaborative instrument that augments rather than replaces clinical judgment. Realising this potential depends on sustained investment in digital literacy, explainable systems, clinician involvement in design, and equitable institutional infrastructure.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in risk-based auditing of large enterprise taxation
items.abstract: The article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations for applying artificial intelligence (AI) in risk-based audits of large enterprise taxation. The study’s relevance stems from the significant fiscal role of large taxpayers, the complexity of their business transactions, the prevalence of cross-border transactions and transfer pricing practices, and the need to identify tax risks promptly amid the digital transformation of tax administration. The study aims to identify areas for AI application to improve the effectiveness of identifying, assessing, and prioritizing tax risks for large enterprises. Based on an analysis of academic research and international approaches, the study systematizes the key tax risks inherent in large enterprises, including those related to transfer pricing, profit shifting across jurisdictions, transactions involving intangible assets, intra-group financing, corporate income taxation, value-added tax (VAT), and tax compliance. The study explores the potential of machine learning, anomaly detection algorithms, predictive analytics, natural language processing (NLP), cluster analysis, and network analysis for processing large volumes of financial and tax data. This study develops a structural and logical model for applying AI in risk-based audits of large enterprise taxation, integrating information and analytical support, AI tools, tax risk profiling, and the auditor’s professional judgment. AI-driven analysis should provide an analytical basis for identifying areas of heightened tax risk and prioritizing audit procedures, while final audit decisions should remain grounded in the auditor’s professional judgment. The practical significance of the findings lies in the potential application of the proposed approach to enhance the validity and effectiveness of risk-based audits of large enterprise taxation. items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Traditional Medical Systems: Emerging Ethical and Governance Challenges for Health Systems
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into traditional medical systems such as Ayurveda and Traditional Chinese Medicine is expanding rapidly, with applications in diagnosis, treatment planning, and decision support. While these developments may improve access and efficiency, they introduce important challenges for healthcare systems, particularly in relation to data quality, clinical validity, regulatory oversight, and practitioner reliance on algorithmic tools. Current governance frameworks largely overlook AI applications in traditional medicine, creating gaps in accountability and quality assurance. This letter highlights key system-level concerns and emphasizes the need for context-specific validation, regulatory clarity, and interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure the safe and effective integration of AI within traditional healthcare practices.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy in Slavonic Studies: Student Reflections
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence literacy is usually assessed through self-report scales. Such instruments show where a group stands, but not how its members reason about the technology in their own terms. Research on this topic has also concentrated on science and technology disciplines and on high-resource languages. It remains unclear how students working in low-resource languages, such as the Slavonic languages, articulate their artificial intelligence literacy, and what knowledge underlies their evaluative judgments. This study analyses written reflections and a background questionnaire from students of Slavonic studies, translation and language teaching who completed a one-semester course in artificial intelligence literacy. The reflections were produced after students used a generative artificial intelligence tool as both the commissioner and the collaborator of an individual academic project. They were examined through qualitative content analysis combining deductive and inductive categories. The findings show that the reflections centre overwhelmingly on evaluating outputs, while declarative knowledge of how such systems function remains a knowledge of symptoms rather than of mechanisms. Evaluative judgments depend heavily on disciplinary expertise in areas such as phonetics, lexicology, translation and language pedagogy, rather than on general critical thinking, and target precisely the errors a domain-uninformed reader would not detect. The questionnaire further shows that students already held a critical disposition toward artificial intelligence before the course began, which constrains how the reflective practice documented here can be interpreted. Taken together, the results reposition disciplinary expertise, more than technical understanding of artificial intelligence, as the primary resource for critical evaluation, with direct implications for teaching artificial intelligence literacy and language technology in higher education.

items.title: ASCENT: Online Test-Time Training of Long-Horizon Agents via Self-Distillation of Verified Experience
items.abstract: A large language model (LLM) agent solves long-horizon tasks through many reasoning-action turns, with one verification signal at termination. Deployed agents face streams of related tasks, making their trajectories a natural resource for improvement. In-context adaptation agents store reflections, memories, or skills as text, so reuse depends on retrieving the right experience and on a frozen policy executing it. We study Online Agentic Test-Time Training (OaTTT), which trains the LLM's weights on its own execution trajectories during deployment. The agent executes each task once, in one pass over the stream, and the executed trajectory with its verification result is the only learning signal for weight updates that persist across tasks. Directly imitating or reinforcing the generated tokens of this single attempt destabilizes the policy. We introduce ASCENT (Agentic Self-distillation for Cross-task EvolutioN at Test-time), which instead self-distills verified experience. A stable version of the LLM, its frozen initial copy, receives the verified trajectory as privileged information and predicts next-token distributions along it with this hindsight. Distilling them into persistent LoRA fast weights updates the agent for later tasks, without an external reference solution or stronger teacher. By further removing invalid-action turns, ASCENT distills enhanced privileged experience for more efficient execution. We characterize its population target and the limits of sparse outcome selection. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and AppWorld at varied model scales, ASCENT improves task success and interaction efficiency as experience accumulates, outperforms online adaptation methods, and transfers to held-out scenes, showing that an agent can consolidate verified experience into its weights without a separate training phase or memory retrieval. items.title: Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems
items.abstract: Agentic machine learning engineering (MLE) is an emerging AI4SE application for complex ML tasks and a step toward recursive self-improvement of AI systems. Recent agentic MLE systems show the value of leveraging insights from related MLE tasks: some systems condition code generation on expert domain knowledge, which is implicitly curated from peer MLE tasks; some systems have a loop of solving an MLE task, gathering memory to benefit future tasks. However, insight collection and injection remain ad hoc, and existing evaluations often do not control insight sources, making data leakage a threat to validity. To close these gaps, we systematically study how insights from related MLE tasks affect agentic MLE systems, and how their impact depends on insight type and injection method. We introduce MLE-InsightBench, a benchmark of 160 Kaggle competitions across 12 domains. To prevent leakage, one competition per domain is held out as the target, while the remaining 148 serve as sources only when they cannot have been influenced by the target task, such as through later editions or reused solutions. We also develop MLE-InsightForge, an insight assembly agent that explores source competitions, top human solutions, and writeups to construct three insight types: 12 domain insights summarizing best practices, 148 competition insights describing winning solutions, and 16 improvement insights capturing generic debugging and optimization strategies. These insights are injected either as on-demand skills or as an upfront playbook. In our evaluation, the extracted insights improve the normalized private-test score by 123.9% over a no-insight baseline. Controlled experiments further show that the three insight types are complementary; the better injection mode (skill vs. playbook) varies by tasks, with skills more cost-effective overall; and the gains generalize across backend LLMs.

items.title: Atomic‐Layer Materials for Energy Storage Systems
items.abstract: Atomic-layer materials (ALMs) provide a promising platform for electrochemical energy storage because their atomically thin structures and interfaces enable control over ion adsorption, charge transfer, diffusion pathways, and interfacial stability. In this review, ALMs include both intrinsic two-dimensional (2D) materials and atomic-layer-engineered functional coatings and interphases produced by atomic layer deposition (ALD), molecular layer deposition (MLD), or related approaches. This work connects atomic-scale design variables, including atomic-scale structural parameters, with device-level performance, degradation, and manufacturability. Their sustainability in batteries and supercapacitors (SCs) will be the main focus. Particular attention is given to how these variables regulate interfacial electrochemical phenomena, metal-ion deposition, and mechanical stability. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are discussed as ALM-specific tools for screening and optimizing ALD/MLD coating chemistry and deposition conditions. Although ALMs offer advantages in laboratory results, practical deployment remains limited by techno-economic bottlenecks or industrial scalability barriers for 2D material processing and device integration. Near-term commercialization is promising for high-leverage interfacial-modification functions in batteries and integrated micro-energy-storage devices. This review also provides a manufacturing framework for discussing the development of durable, scalable, and AI-enabled ALM-based energy-storage technologies.

items.title: Belief-Trajectory Energy: Measuring the Path to a Prediction
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) progressively revise their predictions across Transformer layers, yet we typically observe only the final output, discarding the trajectory through which it is formed. We introduce Belief-Trajectory Energy(BTE), a model-grounded measure that characterizes an input through the layerwise predictive revisions it induces in a model. By mapping intermediate states into a shared predictive space, BTE provides a principled measure of belief change that can be summarized as either a scalar or a structured depth profile. Theoretically, we show that local BTE corresponds to predictive revision under the Fisher-Rao geometry, while the sequence of revisions captures information beyond the initial-to-final belief change. Empirically, scalar BTE provides a model-relative signal of difficulty across diverse reasoning tasks, while richer BTE representations support human-LLM review detection and fine-grained generator attribution, reaching up to $0.998$ macro-AUROC and $95.6\%$ eight-way attribution accuracy. Further analysis shows that BTE develops throughout pretraining and is selectively reshaped by targeted training, demonstrating that the resulting measurement reflects what the scoring model has learned. Together, our results establish belief trajectories as a principled model-grounded signal and suggest a broader perspective in which learned models can themselves serve as instruments for characterizing the data they process. More demonstrations can be found at https://yingjiahao14.github.io/BTE-web/.

items.title: Between Determinism and Chance: From Llull's Machine to Generative AI Models
items.abstract: In 1937, Jorge Luis Borges looked back some 650 years at Ramon Llull‘s machinic ars inveniendi. This is one of five essays that looks at contemporary learning machines through the lens of Borges‘s characteristically engimatic historical note and literary reflection. It examines the epistemological tension between determinism and randomness in projects of formalising thought – from Ramon Llull's Ars Magna (1305) to contemporary generative transformers. Borges's 1937 critique of Llull revealed a fundamental impasse: closed combinatorial systems, lacking contextual sensitivity, produce syntactic noise rather than truth. Yet Borges proposed an alternative, namely, to use such machines as generators of random combinations subject to human selection. This shift finds unexpected validation in AI transformer models. By replacing discrete symbols with continuous semantic embeddings and dynamic attention mechanisms, transformers overcome Llull's linear blindness. However, in deterministic mode (low temperature), they merely reproduce linguistic clichés, exhibiting neural text degeneration. Genuine novelty emerges only through stochastic sampling–temperature-based deviation into the probability distribution's long tail, actualising latent semantic projections (as in the Borgesian “red tiger”). Drawing on recent empirical studies, the paper demonstrates a fundamental trade-off between alignment due to reinforcement learning (RLHF) and stochastic creativity. As an alternative, calibrated uncertainty is proposed, allowing models to acknowledge the limits of knowledge. The transformer that legitimises its stochastic nature thereby approaches Borges's ideal of a poetic machine – an instrument that does not prove but suggests, that does not close off truth but opens a space for play.

items.title: BEYOND "JUST USE AI": A TEACHER-MEDIATED FRAMEWORK FOR MEANINGFUL AI INTEGRATION IN EFL CLASSROOMS — INSIGHTS FROM REAL TEACHING AND MULTI-AI PRACTICE IN UZBEKISTAN
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly present in English language learning, yet easier access to explanations, models, and feedback does not automatically produce stronger learning. This practice-informed paper examines AI use through real English teaching and material-development experience in Uzbekistan, including examination-oriented reading, writing, speaking, vocabulary, and grammar work. It proposes the TRUST framework—Target, Run, Use, Scrutinize, Transfer—as a teacher-mediated model that keeps learners cognitively active before, during, and after AI interaction. The paper also introduces the AI-free moment as a practical check of independent learning.

items.title: Beyond Task Completion: Measuring Interaction Cost in Terminal User Interfaces
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used through terminal user interfaces (TUIs), yet task completion alone does not capture how difficult an interface is to understand and operate. Existing human assessments and LLM-generated ratings or reports do not provide repeatable measurements of interaction effort grounded in verified task execution. We propose Agent-as-a-User, an evaluation paradigm that places an LLM agent in the user role. Agent-KLM separates agent-side interpretation and operation costs and relates them structurally to human interaction. TUINaut operationalizes the paradigm by recording interaction trajectories and verifying outcomes with actor-independent oracles. Using TUINaut-Bench, we study 84 tasks across 15 real-world TUIs with six human participants and five observation-evaluator configurations, and evaluate 45 TUIs generated by three leading stacks. Similar aggregate success rates mask differences in which tasks humans and agents complete, whereas interpretation and operation costs follow correlated task rankings, especially for operation. This pattern persists across configurations. Generated TUIs can implement correct functionality while still requiring usability improvements. These results position Agent-as-a-User as a repeatable, execution-grounded paradigm for measuring task-based usability.

items.title: Beyond the algorithm
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly integrated into occupational health medicine practice, offering potential improvements in diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. However, their implementation introduces novel challenges, including algorithmic bias, lack of transparency in decision-making processes, and risks of over-reliance on automated outputs without appropriate clinical judgment. As occupational health decisions directly affect both individual worker protection and broader workplace public health, professionals must develop advanced information literacy that extends beyond traditional source evaluation to include a critical understanding of AI systems themselves, including their underlying data sources, technical limitations, and potential biases. This study evaluated AI information literacy among 16 occupational health professionals (specialists and residents) participating in the EASOM Summer School 2025. A five-item knowledge-based assessment adapted to occupational health contexts evaluated participants' competencies in identifying biased research questions, selecting evidence retrieval strategies, assessing the accuracy of AI-generated content, applying ethical AI use practices, and understanding proper citation protocols. Overall mean quiz performance was 2.56/5 points (SD = 1.09), indicating substantial gaps in AI information literacy. Questions assessing biased research design yielded the poorest performance (12.5% correct), while questions on ethical AI use in academia (81.2% correct) and citation practices (68.8% correct) demonstrated higher competency. Age showed significant negative correlation with quiz scores (ρ = −0.511, p = 0.043), suggesting younger professionals are better prepared for AI-integrated practice. These findings, although comprised from a small sample, demonstrate the need for targeted educational interventions addressing algorithmic bias recognition, critical question formulation, and responsible AI integration in occupational health medicine practice and worker protection.

items.title: Bridging the Digital Learning Divide: Artificial Intelligence, Access, and the Social Determinants of Higher Education Outcomes in Africa
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence into African higher education has renewed the expectation that technology will close long-standing gaps in educational opportunity. This study argues that the expectation will be disappointed unless the digital learning divide is understood as a socially structured condition, and not merely as a question of who owns a device or holds a connection. The study adopts a conceptual-analytical design based on theoretical adaptation and synthesis rather than primary data. Sources were selected purposively from the sociology of the digital divide, the social determinants of health framework, and fundamental cause theory. Constructs were retained only where the valued outcome is influenced by flexible resources and the mechanisms producing it change over time, and were then applied to artificial intelligence in African higher education using recent continental connectivity evidence. The analysis yields a three-tier social determinants model of higher education outcomes, in which structural determinants, intermediary determinants, and differential digital access, use and outcome operate together, bound by flexible resources that generate cumulative advantage. Within this model, artificial intelligence amplifies opportunity where infrastructure, preparation, support and governance are present, and amplifies disadvantage where they are absent. Interventions confined to access are therefore absorbed without disturbing the achievement gradient, and average effects can conceal a widening distributional gap. Governments and institutions should fund the enabling conditions as components of any artificial intelligence programme; target the achievement gradient through proportionate universalism; subject classifying systems to equity audit, explanation, contestation and data protection; and ground platforms in local context, language and participation. Bridging the digital learning divide is a task of social redistribution, not only of technological supply. Keywords: digital access; digital skills; artificial intelligence adoption; socioeconomic status; higher education outcomes; educational equity

items.title: Building LLM Agent Systems the Deep Learning Way: From Modular Design to Architecture Search
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized AI research and enabled exciting agent systems. To build a complex LLM agent system, most existing research relies on insights from other domains or heuristics to manually build the agent system. However, this approach often requires heavy hand-engineering and fails to fully optimize for the downstream task of interest. Inspired by the tremendous success of deep learning, we propose to construct LLM agent systems in a modular manner, similar to building a deep neural network. Our key insight is to make analogies between LLM building blocks, such as retrievals, memories, and prompting strategies, and the successful deep learning modules, such as MLPs, attention, and recurrent modules. We further design forward inference and feedback mechanisms for LLMs, where prompts in LLMs are considered as the weights in deep models, and the prompt optimization from feedback is analogous to the back-propagation algorithm. We additionally leverage a search algorithm to search for the best configuration of LLM agent systems, similar to the neural architecture search (NAS) in deep learning research. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed deep learning recipe for LLM agent systems is highly effective, in particular: (1) Organizing LLM modules into deep-learning-style architectures yields noticeable performance gain; (2) Automatic prompt optimization, equivalent to backpropagation, is efficient in incorporating feedback from the task of interest and achieves at least 5% performance improvement; (3) NAS equivalent algorithm works well for further optimizing the LLM agent system architecture with 11% performance gain compared with randomly designed architectures. Overall, our research demonstrates the exciting opportunity of transferring the success of deep learning to building LLM agent systems.

items.title: Claiming sociodigital futures? Knowledge practices and their consequences
items.abstract: There is currently intense and widespread speculation about the implications of digital technologies for future societies, despite a wealth of evidence that past claims to predict how technology will shape the future have usually failed. Nonetheless, it is now well established that claims to knowledge about how emerging technologies will shape future worlds are performative, exercising powerful effects on the futures they claim to describe. Building on the Sociology of Expectations and work on Sociotechnical Imaginaries, this paper turns attention to the ontological and epistemological ‘nuts’ and ‘bolts’ of claims about digital technologies, social life and the future. We ask: how are these entities and the relations between them constituted and given traction as knowledge practices? Specifically, we explore the practices used by major future-claiming institutional actors in a selection of published documents. We find a strikingly coherent ontological performance of the relations between ‘the digital’, ‘the social’ and ‘the future’ and the circulation of (what comes to count as) knowledge across these institutions. Indeed, what is striking is the re-purposability of these knowledge practices despite the distinctive institutional interests in play. These knowledge practices offer a limited grasp on the futures that are currently in the making. Moreover, they enable the persistence of a latent set of assumptions which are powerful in limiting consideration of critical questions about the future.

items.title: CodeForge-MA: Execution-Verified Multi-Agent Learning with Language-Conditioned LoRA for Multilingual Code Generation
items.abstract: Large language models for code generation often fail on execution, multilingual coverage, and contamination control, especially under frozen backbone constraints. We present CodeForge-MA, a unified framework that improves code synthesis through a multi-agent data forge, execution verified reinforced instruction tuning, and a language conditioned mixture of LoRA adapters. Four specialized agents, Composer, Reviewer, Executor, and Curator, iteratively refine instruction code pairs, validate them with tests, and filter duplicates and benchmark leakage. During training, we combine masked supervised fine tuning with a test driven reinforcement objective to align generations with executable correctness. For the larger model, we use sparse expert routing over low rank adapters to improve cross language transfer while keeping the base model unchanged at inference. Experiments show that joint data, objective, and adapter design yields robust gains across programming languages.
